# Results {#sec-results}

This section presents the numerical and empirical results of the study. First, we outline the experimental setup for both the synthetic and real-world datasets. Next, we demonstrate the point and probabilistic forecasting performances of the candidate methods considered. We then evaluate their operational utility by presenting their inventory performances in terms of the inventory burden versus the service level achieved (the efficiency frontier), ultimately combining these metrics using a URS. Lastly, we translate these inventory outcomes into tangible public health impacts and provide extensive model diagnostics to define the boundary conditions of our approach.

## Numerical experiment setup

To evaluate the proposed framework in a fully controlled setting, we developed a synthetic dataset that emulates the structural features and disruptions commonly observed in contraceptive demand across FPSC settings. The objective was twofold: (1) to test the model’s ability to recover latent demand under known censorship scenarios, and (2) to assess how forecasting improvements translate into inventory outcomes when the true demand is known.

We generated 1,000 monthly time series, representing 100 stores and 10 products, each with 100 observations. The series were designed to replicate the main demand patterns observed in our empirical data following the classical intermittent demand taxonomy of @syntetos2005. This ensured that the synthetic environment reflected the diversity of demand behaviours found in FPSC operations.

To control variability, each type was assigned a target coefficient of variation (CV) drawn from empirically realistic ranges. Noise processes were selected to match the characteristics of contraceptive demand: AR(1) structures to capture short‐term autocorrelation, and Student‐$t$ innovations to allow for bursty, heavy‐tailed behaviour (@koehler2012). To mimic cross‐series dependencies, we embedded shared seasonal patterns and common shock components within subsets of series, reflecting the correlated responses often seen across products or facilities.

We explicitly modelled supply‐side disruptions by introducing behavioural anomalies and censorship events. These included service interruptions (full censorship), partial stockouts (observed demand proportionally reduced), and cold‐start periods with no recorded issues but zero demand issuance. By varying the type and intensity of these disruptions, the synthetic setup provides a controlled test bed for evaluating the ability of TCKF to recover latent demand under realistic and challenging FPSC conditions. Full details of the data generation logic, including sampling procedures, censoring rules, and distributional assumptions, are provided in **E-Companion, Section 5.** 

@fig-ts_feat1 summarises the key timeseries features of the synthetic dataset used in the numerical experiment.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ts_feat1
#| cache: true
#| out.width: "70%"
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Timeseries characteristics of the synthetic dataset used in the numerical experiment."
#| fig-subcap: "Representative time series; (b) distribution of series by trend and seasonality strength; (c) intermittency classification using IDI and CV^2 thresholds."


# pick one series per (category × type)

synthetic_tsb <- read_rds(here::here('data/tidy_data/synthetic_data.rds'))

idi_stat <- function(x){
  nz <- which(x > 0); if (length(nz) < 2) return(NA_real_); mean(diff(nz))
}
cv2_pos <- function(x){
  y <- x[x > 0]; if (length(y) < 2) return(NA_real_); (sd(y)/mean(y))^2
}

synthetic_feat <- synthetic_tsb |>
  features(observed_demand, feat_stl)

idi_cv2 <- synthetic_tsb  |> 
  as_tibble()  |>   
  group_by(series_category, series_type, store, product) |> 
  summarise(
    IDI = idi_stat(observed_demand),   
    CV2 = cv2_pos(observed_demand),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

selected <- tibble(
  store = c("S84", "S7", "S48"),
  product = c("P3", "P10", "P4")
)

# grab the full time‐slice for those series

plot_df <- synthetic_tsb |>
  semi_join(selected, by = c("store","product")) |> 
  group_by(store, product) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(period = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()


# build shading rectangles for each contiguous run of censorship

shade_df <- plot_df |>
  as_tibble() |> 
  arrange(store, product, period) |>
  group_by(store, product) |>
  mutate(
    run_id = cumsum(
      c(TRUE, censorship_type[-1] != censorship_type[-n()])  
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(store, product, run_id, censorship_type) |>
  summarize(start = min(period), end = max(period), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(censorship_type != "none")

# plot

p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = shade_df,
    aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = censorship_type), 
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.25) +
  
  geom_rect(data = shade_df |>
              filter(start == end),
            aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, colour = censorship_type),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = NA,
            size = 0.5, alpha = 0.05, show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  geom_line(data = plot_df,
            aes(x = period, y = actual_demand, colour = "Actual", linetype = "Actual"),
            linewidth = 0.75) +
  
  geom_line(data = plot_df,
            aes(x = period, y = observed_demand, colour = "Observed", linetype = "Observed"),
            linewidth = 0.75) +
  
  facet_wrap(~product, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Censorship type",
    values = c(censored = "#E69F00", disruption = "#0072B2"),
    labels = c(censored = "Stockout", disruption = "Interruption")) +
  
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Demand", 
                      values = c(Actual = "black", Observed = "red", censored = "#E69F00", disruption = "#0072B2"),
                      breaks = c("Actual", "Observed")) +
  
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Demand",values = c(Actual = "solid", Observed = "dashed")) +
  
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Demand", caption = '(a)') +
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_family = "Assistant", base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.border       = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA),
    panel.spacing      = unit(0.5, "lines")
  )

# ts feat

p2 <- synthetic_feat |>
  mutate(product = factor(product,
                          levels = c('P1', 'P2', 'P3', 'P4', 'P5', 'P6', 'P7', 'P8', 'P9', 'P10'))) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x= trend_strength, y = seasonal_strength_year, color = product)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.75) + 
  labs(x = "Strength of trend", y = "Strength of seasonality", color = 'Product code', caption = '(b)') +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "D") + 
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_family = "Assistant", base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.border       = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA),
    panel.spacing      = unit(0.5, "lines")
  )

# cv2

p3 <- idi_cv2 |>
  mutate(product = factor(product,
                          levels = c('P1', 'P2', 'P3', 'P4', 'P5', 'P6', 'P7', 'P8', 'P9', 'P10'))) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x= IDI, y = CV2, color = product)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.75) + 
  # threshold lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4/3, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +

  # add text labels right next to the lines
  annotate("text",
           x    = 4/3,
           y    = 20,
           label = "IDI = 4/3",
           hjust = -0.1,          # nudge it just to the right
           vjust =  0,          # and align at the top
           size  = 4,
           family = "Assistant") +
  annotate("text",
           x    = max(idi_cv2$IDI, na.rm = TRUE),
           y    = 2.5,
           label = "CV² = 0.5",
           hjust =  1.1,          # nudge it to the right edge
           vjust = 1.1,          # nudge it a bit above the line
           size  = 4,
           family = "Assistant") +

  # force the axes to include those exact ticks
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::extended_breaks()(c(0, max(idi_cv2$IDI))),
                     minor_breaks = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::extended_breaks()(c(0, max(idi_cv2$CV2))),
                     minor_breaks = NULL) +

  labs(x = "IDI",
       y = expression(CV^2),
       caption = '(c)') +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "D", guide = FALSE) + # Use the viridis palette
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_family = "Assistant", base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.border       = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA),
    panel.spacing      = unit(0.5, "lines")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 22))

p1 / (p2 | p3) +  
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")


```

Panel (a) shows three indicative time series representing different product-level demand behaviours. We include both the actual demand (black) and the observed demand (red dashed), highlighting periods of censorship due to stockouts (yellow) and service interruptions (blue). As shown, observed demand systematically understates the true underlying signal in both cases, a pattern we frequently observe in LMIS data. These examples illustrate the conditions under which our proposed method is designed to recover true demand.

Panel (b) explores the strength of trend and seasonality across all 1,000 generated time series, extracted using the STL decomposition method [@cleveland1990]. Each dot represents one time series, with values scaled between 0 and 1. As intended, the dataset includes a wide variety of combinations, from strong trend and weak seasonality to low-trend, low-seasonality patterns. This mirrors the real-world contraceptive demand environment, where seasonal signals are often weak or inconsistent (see @fig-ts_feat2).

Panel (c) categorises time series based on intermittency (IDI) and demand variability ($CV^2$), using the thresholds defined in @kostenko2006. We follow the standard convention, where $IDI > 4/3$ and $CV^2 \leq 0.5$ is considered ‘intermittent’. In our case, most series fall into the erratic or lumpy categories, which aligns with the empirical patterns we aim to replicate, especially where demand bursts, cold starts, or zero-issuance periods are common.

## Empirical experiment setup using real world data

For our empirical evaluation, we used monthly data collected from the LMIS of Côte d’Ivoire, covering the period from January 2016 to December 2019. \rev{The dataset includes 507 time series across nine contraceptive products, spanning product categories in both male and female condoms, emergency contraceptives, oral pills, injectables, implants, and IUDs.} Our target variable is the quantity of stock distributed, which we treat as the observed demand. During initial checks, we found no duplicated values. However, a few healthcare sites reported new product introductions during the time window. For these, we imputed zeros prior to the product's first appearance, based on metadata and comment fields recorded by the site-level demand planners.

To identify censored demand, we used two main sources: the “stockout days” field, and comment logs written by demand planners. These included notes on stockouts, facility closures, delivery delays, untrained staff, stockouts at upstream warehouses, and other service disruptions. Using these, we constructed two binary indicators: one for stockouts and another for service interruptions.

@fig-ts_feat2 shows the timeseries characteristics of the real-world dataset. 

```{r}
#| include: false

# pick one series per (category × type)

stock_tsb <- read_rds(here::here('data/tidy_data/stock_tsb_filtered.rds')) |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(censorship_type = case_when(stock_out_indicator == 1 ~ 'censored',
                                     interruption_indicator == 1 ~ 'disruption',
                                     .default = 'none'),
         censorship_type = as.factor(censorship_type)) |> 
  select(date, site_code, product_code, censorship_type,
         stock_initial, stock_receieved, stock_distributed, stock_adjustment, stock_end,
         projected_average_monthly_consumption, stock_required , stock_ordered, corrected_cmm) |> 
  as_tsibble(index = date, key = c(site_code, product_code)) |> 
  fill_gaps(.full = TRUE) |>  # add zeros to cold staters
  mutate(censorship_type = replace_na(censorship_type, 'none'),
         across(where(is.numeric), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)),
         model = 'system_gen')

idi_stat <- function(x){
  nz <- which(x > 0); if (length(nz) < 2) return(NA_real_); mean(diff(nz))
}
cv2_pos <- function(x){
  y <- x[x > 0]; if (length(y) < 2) return(NA_real_); (sd(y)/mean(y))^2
}

stock_feat <- stock_tsb |>
  features(stock_distributed, feat_stl)

idi_cv2 <- stock_tsb  |> 
  as_tibble()  |>   
  group_by(site_code, product_code) |> 
  summarise(
    IDI = idi_stat(stock_distributed),   
    CV2 = cv2_pos(stock_distributed),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Panel (a) presents four representative time series. Although we only show stock distributed (i.e., observed demand), we can already observe irregular and intermittent patterns, similar to those in the synthetic dataset. Panel (b) plots trend strength against seasonality strength, with each point representing a time series. In contrast to the synthetic data, most real-world series show moderate to low seasonality and a wider spread in trend strength. Panel (c) classifies time series based on $IDI$ and $CV^2$. Most of the series fall into the intermittent and lumpy categories, with only a small proportion appearing smooth or erratic.

```{r}
    avg_I = round(mean(avg_I, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    L = round(mean(L, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

inv_metrics_emp_summary <- inv_metrics_emp |>
  group_by(policy, model, lambda) |>
  summarise(
    CSL = round(mean(CSL, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    stockout_rate = round(mean(stockout_rate, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    I_norm = round(mean(I_norm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    avg_I = round(mean(avg_I, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    L = round(mean(L, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


```

In the numerical experiment, we compare the relative forecast performance of all candidate models against the TCKF benchmark. @tbl-num_fc_acc reports the mean FVA for point forecasts and the mean Skill Score for different quantile levels. Across both point and probabilistic forecasts, none of the benchmark models achieves a positive mean FVA or mean Skill Score. This indicates that, on average, no method adds value relative to TCKF in the synthetic setting.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-num_fc_acc
#| tbl-cap: "Overall forecast performance, expressed as mean FVA and mean Skill Scores, in the numerical experiment. Best values in each column are highlighted in bold."

set_to_bold_max <- function(tbl, cols = 2:6, digits = 3) {
  df <- as.data.frame(tbl, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cols <- cols[cols <= ncol(df)]
  if (length(cols) == 0) return(df)
  
  for (i in cols) {
    # try numeric conversion (silently)
    vec_num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(df[[i]])))
    
    # if whole column non-numeric -> make blanks and skip
    if (all(is.na(vec_num))) {
      df[[i]] <- rep("", nrow(df))
      next
    }
    
    # use rounded values for display and tie detection
    rounded <- round(vec_num, digits)
    
    # mask for best (maximum). handle NA safely
    best_mask <- !is.na(rounded) & rounded == max(rounded, na.rm = TRUE)
    
    # formatted strings (blank for NA)
    fmt <- paste0("%.", digits, "f")
    formatted <- ifelse(is.na(rounded), "", sprintf(fmt, rounded))
    
    # bold all best entries
    formatted[best_mask] <- paste0("\\textbf{", formatted[best_mask], "}")
    
    df[[i]] <- formatted
  }
  
  return(df)
}
```

In the empirical evaluation, we assess forecast performance using uncensored observations only, so that accuracy reflects periods where demand is observed without distortion from stockouts or interruptions. @tbl-fc_acc shows the same overall pattern: no method improves on TCKF in either FVA or Skill Scores. However, model behaviour changes in the real setting. Linear Regression, which is comparatively competitive in the synthetic experiment, performs substantially worse empirically. This is consistent with the empirical data characteristics. Most series exhibit moderate-to-low seasonality, and many are intermittent with low overall demand. These features reduce the advantage of models that rely on strong trend or seasonal structure and favour approaches that remain stable under sparse and irregular demand.

The LMIS system-generated forecast performs similarly to simple mean-based baselines, which is acceptable as a reference point, but it remains far from TCKF. Demand planner adjustments consistently reduce forecast accuracy relative to the system forecast. From a pure forecasting standpoint, these adjustments do not add value. However, it remains important to see how these adjustments affect inventory outcomes, since they may still serve operational purposes beyond forecast error minimisation.

To test whether differences in forecast performance are statistically meaningful, we apply the Nemenyi post-hoc test at the 5% level using inverted FVA values (i.e., $(1-\text{FVA})$, which is equivalent to a relative RMSE scale). This transformation is needed because the Nemenyi procedure ranks methods from smallest to largest values, whereas higher FVA indicates better performance. By inverting FVA, better models have smaller values and therefore better (lower) ranks, making the ranking direction consistent with the test.

@fig-fva_nemenyi presents the results as a critical-difference style rank plot for the numerical (left) and empirical (right) experiments. Each method is shown with its average rank, and the horizontal bar indicates the 95% confidence interval for that rank. The shaded grey band marks the 95% confidence interval of the best-ranked method. Any method whose confidence interval overlaps this grey band is not significantly different from the top performer; methods whose intervals lie fully outside the band are significantly worse.

Across both settings, TCKF achieves the best (lowest) average rank and its grey-band interval does not overlap with any other method, indicating that TCKF is significantly better than all alternatives at the 5% level.  In the numerical experiment, SBA ranks relatively well compared to many benchmarks, which is notable given its design for intermittent demand and consistent with the high intermittency embedded in the synthetic data. In several model families (e.g., Mean and ARIMA), adding censorship information improves performance relative to their uncensored variants, suggesting that explicitly encoding censored-period structure can reduce bias in demand estimation. The same pattern is weaker for LightGBM, where the censored version offers only marginal improvement.

## Inventory performance

\rev{We now examine how differences in forecast accuracy translate into inventory outcomes. To establish a theoretical upper bound, we first benchmark against an Oracle policy that possesses perfect foresight of the true latent demand. Interestingly, as shown in} @tbl-num_inv_per, \rev{the Oracle achieves a Cycle Service Level (CSL) of 0.97 rather than a perfect 1.00 in the numerical setting. This occurs because, despite perfect foresight, the system remains bounded by physical operational constraints (e.g., the one-month lead time and non-negative ordering limits), establishing 0.97 as the true achievable service ceiling.

We begin our evaluation of the forecasting methods with the deterministic order-up-to policy, which reflects current practice in Côte d’Ivoire.} @tbl-num_inv_per \rev{summarises the results, highlighting the critical trade-off between CSL and inventory burden ($I_{norm}$). Under this policy, Censored Linear Regression and TCKF both achieve the highest joint service level (CSL = 0.92) among all candidate methods. However, Censored Linear Regression achieves this at the expense of substantial overstocking, requiring a normalised inventory ($I_{norm}$) of 3.25. In contrast, TCKF maintains this top-tier service level with a significantly leaner inventory footprint ($I_{norm} = 2.75$), effectively avoiding excessive holding costs. Notably, the top-performing statistical methods incorporated censorship type into their model specification, underscoring the importance of explicitly modelling these periods in FPSC forecasting.

Turning to the uncertainty-aware quantile-based policies, TCKF consistently achieves the highest CSL across all target quantiles while maintaining strict inventory efficiency. Furthermore, TCKF exhibits superior probabilistic calibration: as the target quantile increases from 80% to 95%, TCKF smoothly scales its inventory protection ($I_{norm}$ increases from 1.19 to 1.77), yielding proportional improvements in service (CSL increases from 0.83 to 0.90). By contrast, methods such as TimeGPT fail to translate higher safety targets into meaningful service improvements, plateauing at 0.77 CSL despite holding significantly more inventory ($I_{norm} = 2.32$) at the q95 target. Similar robust responsiveness is observed in the myopic policies, where TCKF consistently adapts its inventory position to perfectly reflect the escalating shortage penalty ($k$).}

\rev{Transitioning to the empirical evaluation using the LMIS dataset, we observe that the operational dynamics largely mirror the numerical experiment, although exacerbated by real-world demand volatility and censorship. Here, we observe an interesting phenomenon with the Oracle benchmark, which achieves a perfect CSL of 1.00. This occurs because, to ensure the rigour of the analysis, we excluded censored periods from the empirical performance evaluation. Within these filtered, uncensored periods, the Oracle’s perfect foresight allows it to fully satisfy the observed demand. This highlights why the numerical experiment, where the actual demand is known, is essential for rigorous benchmarking.}

@tbl-inv_per \rev{shows the results for the deterministic order-up-to policy, representing current practice. Demand Planners achieve a near-perfect service level (CSL = 0.99) but do so through unsustainable hoarding, requiring an immense normalised inventory ($I_{norm}$) of 12.82. In resource-constrained FPSC, such levels of overstocking are operationally unviable and may divert life-saving stock away from other facilities in need. TCKF rectifies this inventory bloat, providing highly competitive service (CSL = 0.92) whilst reducing the required inventory footprint by nearly $64\%$ ($I_{norm} = 4.63$).}

\rev{Admittedly, TCKF does not universally dominate every isolated metric in the empirical setting. For instance, the Mean method achieves nominally higher service under the q95 policy (CSL = 0.94). However, this isolated advantage obscures severe operational trade-offs. The Mean method brute-forces service through systematic over-ordering ($I_{norm} = 4.42$ compared to TCKF’s 3.65). Similarly, established heuristics like SBA match TCKF's service level (CSL = 0.92) but require a higher safety stock buffer to do so ($I_{norm} = 3.82$). Ultimately, TCKF delivers the most reliable joint performance, robustly navigating the highly asymmetric trade-off between preventing stockouts and avoiding unsustainable inventory bloat.

The true value of TCKF’s joint performance becomes most apparent under uncertainty-aware quantile policies, which act as a strict stress test for probabilistic calibration. While point-forecast heuristics rely on ad-hoc buffers, foundational models exhibit a complete failure to safely calibrate to empirical volatility. When targeting the 95th percentile, TimeGPT systematically under-protects against uncertainty, stagnating at a severely compromised service level (CSL = 0.81) because its overly narrow intervals fail to generate adequate safety stock ($I_{norm} = 2.91$). By contrast, TCKF’s distribution-free conformal intervals properly capture the empirical risk, smoothly scaling its inventory protection to $I_{norm} = 3.65$ to achieve a reliable 0.92 CSL. Taken together, whether constrained by strict service-level mandates or dynamic economic penalties, TCKF successfully bridges the gap between forecast accuracy and inventory control, confirming its reliability as a highly adaptable decision-support tool.}

## Unified measure of inventory performnace

\rev{In most inventory scenarios, decisions are based on more than one performance measure due to the inherent trade-offs and interactions among them. To evaluate the forecasting models under a single objective, we calculate the URS, adapted from} @petropoulos2019. \rev{By aggregating the relative stockout rate and relative normalised inventory using a quadratic L2 norm, the URS heavily penalises extreme operational deviations, such as severe stockouts or massive overstocking. Because the URS functions as a joint penalty score, lower values indicate superior operational performance. To address the highly asymmetric costs inherent to public health supply chains, we evaluate the mean URS across a spectrum of shortage penalty weights ($w \in \{0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90\}$). To ensure visual clarity, } @fig-urs \rev{plots the mean URS across $w$ for TCKF alongside the operational baselines and primary statistical benchmarks; results for all candidate models are detailed in the **E-Companion, Section 6**.}

```{r}
#| label: fig-urs
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 20
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Evaluating the Unified Relative Score (URS) across varying shortage penalty weights (w) demonstrating the trade-off between relative service level and inventory footprint."

w_vector <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)

model_aggregates_num <- inv_metrics_num_summary |>
  group_by(policy, model) |>
  summarise(
    mean_stockout = mean(stockout_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_Inorm    = mean(I_norm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

grand_averages_num <- model_aggregates_num |>
  group_by(policy) |>
  summarise(
    avg_all_stockout = mean(mean_stockout, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_all_Inorm    = mean(mean_Inorm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

urs_num <- model_aggregates_num |>
  left_join(grand_averages_num, by = c("policy")) |>
  crossing(w = w_vector) |> 
  mutate(
    rel_stockout = mean_stockout / (avg_all_stockout + 1e-6),
    rel_Inorm    = mean_Inorm / (avg_all_Inorm + 1e-6),
    urs = sqrt(w * rel_stockout^2 + (1 - w) * rel_Inorm^2)
  ) |>
  group_by(model, policy, w) |>
  summarise(
    urs_mean = round(mean(urs, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    urs_sd   = round(stats::sd(urs, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups  = "drop"
  )

model_aggregates_emp <- inv_metrics_emp_summary |>
  group_by(policy, model) |>
  summarise(
    mean_stockout = mean(stockout_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_Inorm    = mean(I_norm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

grand_averages_emp <- model_aggregates_emp |>
  group_by(policy) |>
  summarise(
    avg_all_stockout = mean(mean_stockout, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_all_Inorm    = mean(mean_Inorm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

urs_emp <- model_aggregates_emp |>
  left_join(grand_averages_emp, by = c("policy")) |>
  crossing(w = w_vector) |> 
  mutate(
    rel_stockout = mean_stockout / (avg_all_stockout + 1e-6),
    rel_Inorm    = mean_Inorm / (avg_all_Inorm + 1e-6),
    urs = sqrt(w * rel_stockout^2 + (1 - w) * rel_Inorm^2)
  ) |>
  group_by(model, policy, w) |>
  summarise(
    urs_mean = round(mean(urs, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    urs_sd   = round(stats::sd(urs, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups  = "drop"
  )

    panel.border = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA, size = 0.4),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey92", size = 0.35),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

    legend.position = "none",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1a2b48"),
    legend.text = element_text(colour = "#1a2b48")
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = model_shapes)


plot_data <- urs_emp |>
  filter(!policy %in% c("oracle", "capped")) |>
  mutate(
    w = as.numeric(as.character(w)),
    policy = recode(

        "Quantile 85",
        "Quantile 90",

  )

all_models <- unique(plot_data$model)

model_colors <- setNames(rep("#d3d3d3", length(all_models)), all_models)

model_colors[names(distinct_colors)] <- distinct_colors

p2 <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = w, y = urs_mean, color = model, shape = model, group = model)) +
  # geom_line(

  geom_line(

  ) +

  ) +

  labs(
    x = "Penalty Weight for Stockouts (w)",

  ) +

  theme(

(p1 | p2) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

\rev{We first evaluate operational utility within the controlled numerical setting. In low-weight regimes ($w \le 0.50$), where minimising the inventory footprint is the primary mathematical concern, simple statistical averages yield nominally competitive scores because they structurally under-forecast and maintain exceptionally lean profiles. However, as the evaluation aligns with the true operational reality of FPSCs, where stockouts carry severe human repercussions ($w \ge 0.75$), TCKF emerges as the strictly dominant approach. For instance, under the 95th-percentile quantile policy, TCKF achieves a highly superior URS of 0.671 at $w=0.75$ and 0.545 at $w=0.90$.}

\rev{Transitioning to the empirical evaluation, we previously note that because the actual demand is fundamentally unobservable, we explicitly excluded censored periods when computing performance metrics to prevent bias. Consequently, the empirical URS calculations serve as robust proxies of true operational utility.}

@fig-urs \rev{shows a nuanced operational reality: TCKF does not strictly dominate across all isolated inventory policies, particularly under the deterministic rules where simple heuristics often maintain leaner profiles. Furthermore, under extreme shortage-penalty regimes (e.g., $w = 0.90$), the objective function assigns almost no penalty to holding excess inventory. Consequently, approaches that systematically hoard inventory, such as Demand Planners or simple statistical averages (e.g., Mean and Naive), achieve nominally competitive URS values in this specific regime, frequently scoring below 1.0. Under such an extreme weighting, the metric mathematically forgives inventory bloat and rewards the overstocking utilised by these methods to force high service levels. 

However, the true operational value of TCKF lies in its robust consistency across a broader, more practical spectrum. In the balanced to moderately high-risk regimes ($w \in [0.50, 0.75]$), which realistically weigh the severe human consequences of service failures against the physical and financial constraints of donor-funded supply chains, TCKF excels. While naive baselines and manual adjustments fluctuate wildly between extreme leanness and massive inventory bloat depending on the specific policy applied, TCKF consistently navigates this highly asymmetric trade-off. Ultimately, TCKF provides the most reliable joint performance, successfully establishing the necessary probabilistic safety buffers to avert life-threatening stockouts without relying on unsustainable hoarding.}

## Public health metrics

\rev{Inventory performance in FPSC is ultimately judged not only by service levels and efficiency, but by its consequences for public health. Translating stockout rates into public health impact provides a more meaningful lens through which to assess model performance. } @fig-pub_health \rev{presents the relative mCPR loss for each forecast–inventory policy combination, benchmarked against TCKF.}

```{r}
#| label: fig-pub_health
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 20
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "mCRP loss based on relative stockout loss compared to the TCKF."


method_count <- 10
wra_population <- 100000


healthcare_impact_num <- inv_metrics_num_summary |> 
  filter(!policy %in% c('oracle', 'capped')) |> 
  select(model, policy, stockout_rate) |> 
  distinct() |> 
  left_join(inv_metrics_num_summary |> 
              filter(model == 'TCKF') |> 
              select(policy, stockout_rate) |> 
              distinct() |> 
              rename(stockout_rate_bench = stockout_rate),
            by = c('policy')) |> 
  mutate(mcpr_loss = round(0.065 * method_count * (stockout_rate - stockout_rate_bench),3),
         users_lost = mcpr_loss * wra_population,
         maternal_deaths = users_lost / 3153,
         infant_deaths = users_lost / 251,
         abortions = users_lost / 6.46,
         unintended_pregnancies = users_lost / 3.63)


df_rel_num <- healthcare_impact_num |>
  group_by(policy, model) |>
  summarise(mcpr_loss = round(mean(mcpr_loss, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            users_lost = round(mean(users_lost, na.rm = TRUE)),
            infant_deaths = round(mean(infant_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)),
            abortions  = round(mean(abortions, na.rm = TRUE)),
            unintended_pregnancies = round(mean(unintended_pregnancies, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = 'drop') |> 
  mutate(
    policy = factor(
      policy,
      levels = c(
        "deterministic", "myopic (k=5)", "myopic (k=10)", "myopic (k=20)",
        "upper_q80", "upper_q85", "upper_q90", "upper_q95"
      )
    ),
    policy = forcats::fct_recode(
      policy,
      "Deterministic" = "deterministic",
      "Myopic (k=5)"  = "myopic (k=5)",
      "Myopic (k=10)" = "myopic (k=10)",
      "Myopic (k=20)" = "myopic (k=20)",
      "Quantile 80"   = "upper_q80",
      "Quantile 85"   = "upper_q85",
```

\rev{In the numerical evaluation, TCKF consistently minimises mCPR loss across the policy spectrum. While certain candidate methods exhibit nominally low relative mCPR losses under the deterministic order-up-to policy, our prior inventory analysis demonstrates that these apparent health gains are achieved through inventory buffering rather than true forecasting efficiency. When evaluated under tighter, uncertainty-aware policies, the limitations of competing baselines become starkly apparent. The 95th-percentile quantile policy, for instance, serves as a rigorous stress test for probabilistic calibration. Relying on the Mean method, under this policy results in a 0.026 relative mCPR loss, which corresponds to 2,600 fewer women retaining access per a hypothetical 100,000 population. This forecasting failure directly translates into 716 unintended pregnancies, 402 abortions, and 10 infant deaths. By contrast, TCKF properly calibrates to the uncertainty, preventing these losses while maintaining an efficient inventory footprint.}

\rev{Transitioning to the empirical LMIS dataset, the translation of stockout rates reinforces the severe operational divergence identified in our efficiency frontier analysis. Under the existing deterministic policy, current human interventions (Demand Planners) achieve mathematically lower stockout rates than TCKF, thereby generating a nominal gain in users and averting further mCPR loss. However, these gains are driven by disproportionate and unsustainable inventory accumulation ($I_{norm} = 12.82$). In resource-constrained public health networks, such persistent overstocking at individual facilities inevitably diverts life-saving commodities away from other sites in need, rendering it operationally unviable as a systemic solution.}

\rev{To properly assess the operational value of TCKF without the distortion of manual buffering, we benchmark it against current field practice: the established LMIS System-Generated baseline. When exposed to uncertainty-aware environments, such as the 95th-percentile quantile policy, the performance of the System-Generated baseline frequently deteriorates. To illustrate the scale of these differences in a policy-relevant setting, consider the actual demographic reality of Côte d’Ivoire, where an estimated 1.59 million women of reproductive age rely on modern contraceptives. Within this actual population, transitioning from the current System-Generated forecasts to the proposed TCKF framework prevents an additional 24,761 women from losing access to contraception. Using the RHSC Impact Calculator, this substitution translates directly into averting 6,821 unintended pregnancies, 3,833 abortions, and 99 preventable infant deaths. Ultimately, while ad-hoc manual planners occasionally achieve nominally lower mCPR loss through extreme hoarding, TCKF provides the most consistent and reliable joint performance. It successfully establishes the robust probabilistic coverage required to avert severe human repercussions without relying on the prohibitive excess stock holdings observed in current practice. All the results of public health impact are in **E-companion, Section 7**.}

## Model diagnostic

\rev{To evaluate the boundary conditions of TCKF, we first conduct a diagnostic analysis of signal recovery. A primary failure mode of standard forecasting in FPSC is the "spiral-down" effect, where algorithms naïvely process censored demand as actual demand, driving forecasts progressively downward. Using the numerical dataset (where actual demand $y^*_t$ is known), } @fig-model_diag1 \rev{maps TCKF point predictions ($\hat{y}_t$) against actual demand across three operational regimes.}

```{r}
#| label: fig-model_diag1
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3
#| out.height: "35%"
#| fig-cap: "Evaluating signal recovery across different operational disruptions."


tckf_diag <- read_rds(here::here('data/predictions/tckf_diag.rds'))

sku_diagnostics <- tckf_diag |>
  filter(!is.na(yhat)) |>
  filter(censorship_type == 'none') |> 
  group_by(diag_spec, diag_lambda_choice, diag_cp_mode, store, product) |> 
  summarise(
    sku_rmse = sqrt(mean((yhat - actual_demand)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    sku_cov  = mean(actual_demand <= upper_q95, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

diag_summary_plot <- sku_diagnostics |>
  group_by(diag_spec, diag_lambda_choice, diag_cp_mode) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rmse = mean(sku_rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_rmse   = sd(sku_rmse, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    mean_cov  = mean(sku_cov, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_cov    = sd(sku_cov, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

plot_data <- tckf_diag |> 
  filter(!is.na(yhat), !is.na(actual_demand), actual_demand <= 700)  |> 
  mutate(
    censorship_label = case_when(
      censorship_type == "none" ~ "Uncensored (Normal Operations)",
      censorship_type == "censored" ~ "Partial Censorship (Stockouts)",
      censorship_type == "disruption" ~ "Full Censorship (Interruptions)",
      TRUE ~ as.character(censorship_type)
    ),
    censorship_label = factor(censorship_label, 
                              levels = c("Uncensored (Normal Operations)", 
                                         "Partial Censorship (Stockouts)", 
                                         "Full Censorship (Interruptions)"))
  )

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = actual_demand, y = yhat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, color = "#2c3e50", size = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "#e74c3c", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ censorship_label, scales = "free") +
  theme_few(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    x = "True Latent Demand (Numerical Experiment Actuals)",
    y = "TCKF Predicted Demand"
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.border       = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA, size = 0.4),
    panel.grid.major   = element_line(colour = "grey92", size = 0.35),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    axis.title         = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1a2b48"),
    axis.text          = element_text(colour = "#1a2b48"),
    legend.position    = "right",
    legend.title       = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1a2b48"),
    legend.text        = element_text(colour = "#1a2b48")
  )

```

 @fig-model_diag1 \rev{shows a nuanced recovery profile. Because TCKF relies on a structural state-space foundation, it inherently smooths highly erratic demand; consequently, the model tends to underestimate extreme, isolated high-demand spikes during both normal operations and full service interruptions. However, its true operational value lies in neutralising the spiral-down effect. Under partial censorship (stockouts), the truncated Gaussian update successfully pulls predictions upward toward the true latent demand. Furthermore, during full censorship, deliberately skipping the Kalman update preserves the prior state and prevents state collapse. Thus, while TCKF may struggle to capture erratic high-demand outliers, explicitly distinguishing between censorship types is practically effective in preserving an unbiased baseline demand signal.}

```{r}
#| label: fig-model_diag2
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out.height: "25%"
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy–calibration trade-off induced by the internal modelling choices."

ggplot(diag_summary_plot,
       aes(x = mean_rmse, y = mean_cov,
           color = diag_cp_mode, shape = diag_lambda_choice)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(xmin = mean_rmse - 1.96 * se_rmse,
        xmax = mean_rmse + 1.96 * se_rmse),
    height = 0, linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean_cov - 1.96 * se_cov,
        ymax = mean_cov + 1.96 * se_cov),
    width = 0, linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ diag_spec) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean RMSE (Point Accuracy)",
    y = "Empirical 95% Coverage",
    color = "Conformal Mode",
    shape = "Lambda Choice"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "global"  = "#ffb343",
      "rolling" = "#2D68C4"
    )
  ) +
  theme_few(base_family = "Inter", base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.border       = element_rect(colour = "lightgrey", fill = NA, size = 0.4),
    panel.grid.major   = element_line(colour = "grey92", size = 0.35),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    axis.title         = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1a2b48"),
    axis.text          = element_text(colour = "#1a2b48"),
    legend.position    = "right",
    legend.title       = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1a2b48"),
    legend.text        = element_text(colour = "#1a2b48")
  )

```

\rev{Finally, } @fig-model_diag2 \rev{evaluates the accuracy–calibration trade-off induced by TCKF’s internal configuration. First, a parsimonious state specification yields equivalent or superior RMSE relative to full structural models, confirming that excessive complexity is counterproductive for noisy FPSC demand. Second, rolling conformal calibration achieves higher empirical coverage without deteriorating RMSE, proving its ability to adapt to non-stationary errors. Finally, dynamically estimating the uncertainty inflation weight ($\hat{\lambda}$) maintains robust probabilistic coverage whilst keeping point accuracy stable. Together, these diagnostics fully justify the parsimonious, adaptive design of the proposed framework.}
